title: India's Stock Market Faces Its First Annual Loss in a Decade. Foreign Investors Have Already Left.
excerpt: A Reuters poll of 24 analysts finds the Nifty 50 is headed for a yearly decline as $23 billion in foreign capital exits and AI-driven rallies power markets everywhere but India.
body:
India's benchmark equity indices are headed for their first annual decline in more than a decade, a Reuters poll of 24 equity analysts has found, as foreign investors pull out more than $23 billion this year and the country's stock market loses ground to AI-powered rallies elsewhere.

The Numbers Tell a Stark Story

The Nifty 50, already down approximately 8.5 percent this year, is forecast to close 2026 at around 26,000 — a marginal annual decline of roughly 0.5 percent that would mark its first yearly loss since 2015. The BSE Sensex is projected at 84,150 by year-end. Both forecasts were sharply downgraded from a February poll conducted before the U.S.-Israel war with Iran reshaped global markets.

Taiwan this week overtook India to become the world's fifth-largest stock market by capitalisation, driven by a surge in chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. South Korea's AI-laden KOSPI index has surged more than 200 percent in a year. India's heavyweight IT stocks index, by contrast, has fallen by more than a third since December 2024.

Why Foreign Investors Are Leaving

The exodus is being driven by three converging forces. India's valuation premium — the market trades at more than 20 times earnings — has become increasingly difficult to justify when corporate earnings growth remains negligible. Global investors are rotating into cheaper markets with direct exposure to the artificial intelligence boom. And the Iran war has widened India's current account deficit through surging energy prices, making the macro picture less attractive.

"Everyone wants returns at the end of the day. The returns are not there, earnings growth is almost negligible. AI is where the flavour of the town is right now and this is where India — not just we lack it, we are actually on the wrong side," said Rajat Agarwal, Asia equity strategist at Societe Generale.

Foreign portfolio investors have sold more than $23 billion of their Indian holdings so far in 2026, surpassing last year's record outflows. Foreign ownership of Indian equities is now at an all-time low.

The Domestic Safety Net Is Fraying

The one force that has prevented a sharper decline — domestic retail investors pouring money through systematic investment plans — is showing signs of fatigue. SIPs have grown nearly tenfold over the past decade, and domestic institutional investors now own a record share of Indian equities.

"If this hadn't been in place, we would have seen the Nifty at around 19,000 or 20,000 over the last year," said Aman Sethia, head of treasury at Groww.

But analysts warn that a sustained drought in returns could eventually erode retail enthusiasm. A slim majority — 13 of 24 analysts polled — said a further correction was likely over the coming three months.

What This Means for NRI Investors

For the millions of non-resident Indians with exposure to Indian equities through mutual funds, NRE accounts, and direct brokerage accounts, the message is sobering. India's structural growth story has not fundamentally changed — GDP growth remains among the fastest of any major economy — but the market's ability to translate that growth into equity returns has stalled.

Kishan Gupta, director at CD Equisearch, pointed to a deeper concern: "A culture of innovation — that thing is absent in our country." India's corporate sector, he argued, has not done enough to build innovation-led cash flows, particularly in AI, leaving the market without the growth catalysts that are driving valuations elsewhere.

The silver lining: analysts expect a bounce to 27,000 on the Nifty by mid-2027 and 29,000 by end-2027, suggesting that patient investors may still be rewarded — if the Iran war stabilises and corporate earnings recover.
